headline: High risk: shared filesystem and broad write/network privileges make Cursor↔Goose prone to prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading tool misuse by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor and Goose both read/write local files and use MCP, so one agent can place attacker-controlled content where the other may ingest it. Cursor’s shared_state_with_other_instances via local filesystem and Goose’s shared_state via filesystem create a default bridge. No evidence of provenance tracking or isolation is present, so injection is plausible without unusual setup.
conditions: IF either agent reads instructions from files written by the other without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF a shared workspace contains untrusted text that one agent treats as commands, the other can be steered.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of file contents as instructions.
Require manual review of cross-agent files before execution.
Turn off MCP servers not needed for the task.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code and filesystem contents, and both have broad network egress to model providers/MCP servers. Cursor additionally handles clipboard contents, increasing the chance that sensitive material copied into one environment is exposed to the other through the shared filesystem or editor buffers. This is a default-path leakage risk, not just an unusual configuration.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, both agents can access them.
IF clipboard content is pasted into Cursor and then saved to disk, Goose can read it from the filesystem.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate OS users or directories per agent.
Clear clipboard before switching agents.
Restrict network egress where possible.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the same filesystem and modify git state, and both support multiple instances with filesystem-based shared state. That creates a direct race on files and repository metadata in default use. Without locking or orchestration guarantees, concurrent edits, commits, or package installs can overwrite each other and corrupt state.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF both agents modify git state concurrently, repository corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid concurrent package installs or git operations.
requires-engineering: add file and git locking in the orchestrator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor and Goose both have tool-use autonomy, shell execution, and broad network access, so one agent’s output can become the other’s action plan. If Cursor generates a command or patch that Goose accepts without verification, the second agent can amplify a mistake into destructive filesystem or git actions. The pair lacks documented verification gates in the profiles.
conditions: IF Goose executes Cursor-produced commands or patches without review, errors cascade.
IF Cursor treats Goose output as authoritative and auto-runs it in Yolo mode, mistakes can be amplified.
mitigations: Require human review before executing cross-agent outputs.
Disable Yolo mode for shared tasks.
Have each agent summarize and verify the other’s plan before acting.
Limit shell and git permissions during handoffs.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so no strong compliance breach is evidenced. However, both agents handle source code and files, and both send data to model providers/MCP servers, so compliance gaps could arise if regulated data is placed in the shared workspace. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise data flow, not a single-agent issue.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, both agents may process it.
IF one agent’s provider or MCP endpoint has stricter retention than the other, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared repo.
Use separate projects for regulated and unregulated work.
Review provider retention settings for both agents.
Disable unnecessary logging in both tools.
requires-engineering: document and enforce data-handling policy per agent.
